blocks.body:
The primes have a simple combinatorial property: no prime divides another. So do the numbers $n+1, n+2, \dots, 2n$, and so do the numbers with exactly two prime factors. Sets with this property are called primitive. How large can a primitive set be? In a finite range the answer is a pleasant pigeonhole exercise. For infinite sets, the right measure of size turns out to be $\sum 1/(a\log a)$, and Erdős showed in 1935 that this sum is bounded by an absolute constant over all primitive sets.

He later conjectured that the primes give the largest value. Lichtman proved this in 2022. This lesson proves the finite bound and Erdős's theorem, shows why the primes are the natural candidate for the maximum, and states Lichtman's theorem.

blocks.title: Primitive set
blocks.body:
A set $A$ of integers greater than $1$ is primitive if for any two distinct $a, b \in A$, $a \nmid b$. For such $A$ write
$$f(A) = \sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a \log a}.$$

In other words $A$ is an antichain for divisibility. The integer $1$ is excluded because it divides everything (and $\log 1 = 0$).

blocks.title: Primitive sets in a finite range
blocks.body:
Within $\{1, 2, \dots, N\}$ the numbers greater than $N/2$ form a primitive set (if $a < b$ are both $> N/2$ then $b < 2a$, so $a \nmid b$). That gives $\lceil N/2 \rceil$ elements, far more than the roughly $N/\log N$ primes up to $N$. So counting elements is the wrong measure: a primitive set can contain a positive proportion of $[1,N]$, as long as the elements are all of similar size.

The weighted sum $f(A)$ penalises this. For $A = \{n+1, \dots, 2n\}$,
$$f(A) = \sum_{a=n+1}^{2n} \frac{1}{a\log a} \approx \int_n^{2n} \frac{dt}{t \log t} = \log\log(2n) - \log\log n = \log\Big(1 + \frac{\log 2}{\log n}\Big),$$
which tends to $0$. The primes, by contrast, are spread across all scales, and $f(\text{primes}) = \sum_p \frac{1}{p\log p} = 1.6366\ldots$ (the series converges: by Chebyshev's bounds there are $O(x/\log x)$ primes in $[x, 2x]$, each contributing at most $\frac{1}{x\log x}$, so the block $[2^j, 2^{j+1}]$ contributes $O(1/j^2)$, and these add up to a finite amount).

Why the weight $1/(a\log a)$? Over all integers $\sum_{a\le x} 1/(a\log a)$ grows like $\log\log x$, and over a primitive set one may hope to keep only a bounded part of it. With the weight $1/a$ this would fail: $\sum_p 1/p$ diverges.

blocks.title: A primitive subset of {1,...,2n} has at most n elements
blocks.body: Show that a primitive subset of $\{1, 2, \dots, 2n\}$ (here we allow any positive integers, and the same definition of "no element divides another") has at most $n$ elements, and that $n$ is attained.
blocks.solution:
Write each $m \le 2n$ as $m = 2^j u$ with $u$ odd. The odd part $u$ is one of the $n$ odd numbers $1, 3, \dots, 2n-1$. Group $\{1,\dots,2n\}$ into $n$ chains according to the odd part:
$$\{u, 2u, 4u, \dots\} \cap [1, 2n], \qquad u = 1, 3, \dots, 2n-1.$$
Within a chain any two elements divide one another (the smaller divides the larger), so a primitive set contains at most one element from each chain. By the pigeonhole principle it has at most $n$ elements.

The set $\{n+1, n+2, \dots, 2n\}$ is primitive (shown above) and has $n$ elements. So the maximum is exactly $n$. Note that the odd parts of $n+1, \dots, 2n$ are all different: each chain is used exactly once.

blocks.title: Erdős's theorem (1935)
blocks.body: There is an absolute constant $C$ such that every primitive set $A$ satisfies $f(A) = \displaystyle\sum_{a\in A}\frac{1}{a\log a} \le C$.

blocks.title: The key idea: disjoint sets of multiples
blocks.body:
For an integer $a > 1$ let $P(a)$ be its largest prime factor, and attach to $a$ the set
$$M_a = \{ a m : m \ge 1,\ \text{every prime factor of } m \text{ is} \ge P(a) \}.$$
(The condition is empty for $m = 1$, so $a \in M_a$.) For a prime $a = p$, $M_p$ is exactly the set of integers whose smallest prime factor is $p$.

Two facts drive the proof.

1. If $A$ is primitive, the sets $M_a$ ($a \in A$) are pairwise disjoint.
2. $M_a$ has natural density $\dfrac1a \displaystyle\prod_{p < P(a)}\Big(1 - \frac1p\Big)$.

Fact 2 holds because $am \in M_a$ exactly when $m$ has no prime factor below $P(a)$, and the integers with no prime factor below $y$ have density $\prod_{p<y}(1-1/p)$ (by the Chinese remainder theorem they form a periodic set modulo $\prod_{p<y} p$ with that proportion). Fact 1 is a lemma about prime factorisations.

blocks.title: Proof of Erdős's theorem
blocks.body:
Disjointness. Suppose $n \in M_a \cap M_b$ with $a \ne b$ in $A$. List the prime factors of $n$ with multiplicity in increasing order, $q_1 \le q_2 \le \cdots \le q_r$. Since $n = am$ with every prime of $a$ at most $P(a)$ and every prime of $m$ at least $P(a)$, the primes of $a$ come first in this list: $a = q_1 q_2 \cdots q_s$ where $s$ is the number of prime factors of $a$ counted with multiplicity. (If $P(a)$ also divides $m$, the copies of $P(a)$ are interchangeable, so this is still true.) Likewise $b = q_1 \cdots q_t$. If $s \le t$ then $a \mid b$, and if $t \le s$ then $b \mid a$. Either way one divides the other, contradicting primitivity.

Density bound. Let $A' \subseteq A$ be finite. The sets $M_a$, $a \in A'$, are disjoint, each has a natural density, and a finite disjoint union of sets with densities has density equal to the sum, which is at most $1$. So
$$\sum_{a \in A'} \frac1a \prod_{p < P(a)} \Big(1 - \frac1p\Big) \le 1.$$
Since $A'$ was arbitrary, the same holds for $A$.

Mertens. By Mertens' third theorem ([[mertens]]), $\prod_{p \le x}(1 - 1/p) \sim e^{-\gamma}/\log x$; since the product is positive for every $x \ge 2$, there is an absolute constant $c > 0$ with $\prod_{p\le x}(1-1/p) \ge c/\log x$ for all $x \ge 2$. As $P(a) \le a$,
$$\prod_{p < P(a)}\Big(1-\frac1p\Big) \ge \prod_{p \le a}\Big(1-\frac1p\Big) \ge \frac{c}{\log a}.$$
Substituting, $c \sum_{a\in A} \frac{1}{a \log a} \le 1$, so $f(A) \le 1/c$.

blocks.title: The primes give equality in Erdős's density inequality
blocks.body:
Show that for $A$ = the set of primes,
$$\sum_{p} \frac{1}{p}\prod_{q < p}\Big(1 - \frac1q\Big) = 1,$$
where $q$ runs over primes. Interpret this in terms of the sets $M_p$.
blocks.solution:
Write $E(x) = \prod_{q \le x}(1 - 1/q)$. For each prime $p$,
$$\frac1p \prod_{q<p}\Big(1-\frac1q\Big) = \prod_{q<p}\Big(1-\frac1q\Big) - \prod_{q\le p}\Big(1-\frac1q\Big).$$
Summing over $p \le x$, the right side telescopes to $1 - E(x)$. Since $\sum_q 1/q$ diverges, $E(x) \to 0$ (Mertens gives $E(x) \sim e^{-\gamma}/\log x$), so the full sum is $1$.

Interpretation: $M_p$ is the set of integers whose smallest prime factor is $p$, and these sets partition $\{2, 3, 4, \dots\}$. Their densities therefore add up to $1$, the largest value the inequality in the proof allows. In this sense the primes use up all the room. For $x = 10^6$ the partial sum is $1 - E(10^6) \approx 0.9594$.

This is the heuristic behind Erdős's conjecture: the inequality $\sum_a \frac1a\prod_{p<P(a)}(1-1/p) \le 1$ is tight for the primes, and the weight $\frac1a\prod_{p<P(a)}(1-1/p)$ is roughly $e^{-\gamma}/(a\log a)$, so the primes ought to make $f$ as large as possible too. The approximation is only rough, which is why the conjecture took decades.

blocks.title: Lichtman's theorem (2022), the Erdős primitive set conjecture
blocks.body:
For every primitive set $A$,
$$\sum_{a\in A}\frac{1}{a\log a} \le \sum_{p}\frac{1}{p\log p} = 1.6366\ldots$$

blocks.title: About the proof
blocks.body:
Erdős's argument shows that $f(A)$ is bounded, but turning the disjointness of the $M_a$ into the sharp constant $f(\text{primes})$ is much harder, because the factor $\prod_{p<P(a)}(1-1/p)$ is only approximately $e^{-\gamma}/\log a$ and can be far from it when $P(a)$ is much smaller than $a$. Over the years several people pushed the upper bound for $f(A)$ down towards $1.6366$. Lichtman's 2022 proof is a careful refinement of the same multiples-and-densities circle of ideas, combined with sharp explicit estimates for sums over primes. We do not reproduce it.

Related questions remain. For instance, the set $\mathbb{N}_k$ of integers with exactly $k$ prime factors (with multiplicity) is primitive for each $k$, and one can ask how $f(\mathbb{N}_k)$ behaves as $k$ varies; this has been studied in detail by Lichtman and others.

blocks.title: Numerics
blocks.body:
(a) Estimate $\sum_p \frac{1}{p\log p}$ by summing over $p \le 10^7$ and adding an estimate for the tail.

(b) Compute $f(\{n+1, \dots, 2n\})$ for $n = 10, 100, 1000$ and compare with $\log\big(1 + \frac{\log 2}{\log n}\big)$.
blocks.solution:
(a) By the prime number theorem the primes near $t$ have density about $1/\log t$, so the tail is
$$\sum_{p > x} \frac{1}{p\log p} \approx \int_x^\infty \frac{dt}{t \log^2 t} = \frac{1}{\log x}.$$
For $x = 10^7$, $1/\log x \approx 0.0620$. Summing $1/(p\log p)$ over the primes up to $10^7$ and adding $0.0620$ gives $1.6366$, in agreement with the known value $1.63661\ldots$. The slow convergence (the tail decays only like $1/\log x$) is typical of sums over primes.

(b) The sums are approximately $0.2502$, $0.1396$ and $0.0956$ for $n = 10, 100, 1000$, while $\log(1 + \log 2/\log n)$ gives $0.2632$, $0.1402$ and $0.0956$. (For $n = 10$ the integral approximation is still rough.) These primitive sets have $n$ elements, far more than the primes up to $2n$, yet their $f$-value is small and tends to $0$.

blocks.body:
- Primitive sets can be large in cardinality (half of $[1,N]$); boundedness is a statement about the weighted sum $f$, not about counting.
- $\sum_{a\in A} 1/a$ can diverge for primitive $A$ (take the primes); the extra $\log a$ in the weight is essential.
- In the disjointness lemma the condition is that the prime factors of $m$ are at least $P(a)$. With "at most $P(a)$" instead, disjointness fails: $30 = 10\cdot 3 = 15 \cdot 2$ would lie in the sets for both $a = 10$ and $a = 15$.
- The constant from the crude Mertens bound is not the sharp one; Lichtman's theorem is a much finer statement than boundedness.

Primitive sets combine the antichain viewpoint of [[combinatorial-nt]] and [[set-systems|extremal set theory]] (divisibility is a partial order, and the finite bound above is a chain decomposition argument) with the analytic input of [[mertens]] and the [[pnt|prime number theorem]]. The sets $M_a$ are sieve-type objects, close to the "rough numbers" of [[sieve-basics]], and the densities $\prod_{p<y}(1-1/p)$ are the basic quantities of [[probabilistic-nt|probabilistic number theory]].

1. Show that the set of integers with exactly $k$ prime factors counted with multiplicity is primitive, and that the set of integers with exactly $k$ distinct prime factors is not (for $k \ge 1$).
2. Let $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ be primitive with $|A| = n$. Show that $A$ contains exactly one number with each odd part $u \in \{1, 3, \dots, 2n-1\}$.
3. Prove directly from the definition that the sets $M_p$ for primes $p$ partition the integers greater than $1$.
4. Let $A$ be primitive and suppose every element of $A$ has all its prime factors at least $y$. Show that $\sum_{a\in A}\frac1a\prod_{p<P(a)}(1-\frac1p) \le \prod_{p<y}(1-\frac1p)$.
